                       n = as.integer(counts[1:8]))
e1 <- ggplot(top8, aes(pAct, n)) + geom_col(fill = PAL["orange"], width = .7) +
  labs(x = "pActivity", y = "compounds", title = "1. value pile-ups") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, hjust = 1, size = 6))
unit_df <- rbind(data.frame(lv = log10(1000 * um$value), unit = "reported in uM"),
                 data.frame(lv = log10(pmax(nm$value, 1e-2)), unit = "reported in nM")) |>
  filter(is.finite(lv))
e2 <- ggplot(unit_df, aes(lv, colour = unit)) + geom_freqpoly(bins = 25, linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("green", "blue")]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "log10(value in nM)", y = "measurements",
       title = "2. the uM assays are the weak ones") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
repl <- cmpd |> filter(n_exact > 1)
e3 <- ggplot(repl, aes(pActivity, pActivity_range)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.45, colour = PAL["blue"]) +
  geom_point(data = ws, size = 0.9, colour = PAL["orange"]) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = PAL["orange"], linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "median pActivity", y = "max - min among replicates",
       title = "3. replicate disagreement")
print(e1 | e2 | e3)

Figure 16. The three anomalies. (1) The eight most frequent pActivity values, each shared by dozens of compounds. (2) Measurements reported in micromolar against those reported in nanomolar, both converted to nanomolar: the 470 micromolar-reported rows, from 83 assays, sit visibly to the right of the nanomolar ones (medians 1,200 nM against 550 nM) but overlap them heavily — a tendency, not a separation. (3) Replicate disagreement against median potency: 60 compounds (orange) disagree by more than one log unit, the worst by 3.3 — a thousandfold discrepancy between laboratories for the same molecule. Unit 6 turns this scatter into an estimate of the noise floor that caps any model’s accuracy.

Anomaly 2 — the unit a paper uses carries information. Four hundred and seventy raw measurements, from 83 assays in 77 documents, were reported in micromolar rather than nanomolar. Converted to a common unit their median is 1,200 nM against 550 nM for the nanomolar-reported rows — a factor of 2.2, with 52% of the micromolar rows above 1 µM against 40% of the nanomolar ones. The effect is modest and the two distributions overlap heavily, so this is a tendency rather than a clean separation: authors reach for micromolar when the compounds they are describing are weak. The unit is therefore not a neutral formatting choice but a weak proxy for the kind of experiment, worth recording in the data card even though it would be wrong to treat it as a label.

Anomaly 3 — replicate disagreement. Sixty compounds have replicate measurements differing by more than one log unit, with a median disagreement of 1.46 and an extreme case of 3.3. Three of the four worst are named, well-studied inhibitors — GSK-269962A, Y-27632 and belumosudil — measured in up to 20 documents, which is the point: the disagreement grows with the number of independent laboratories, not with the obscurity of the compound. These are not errors to delete; they are the dataset telling you how reproducible it is, and every one of them is an upper bound on how well a model can ever predict that compound.

big <- names(which(table(d$scaffold_smiles) >= 5))
cl <- d |> filter(scaffold_smiles %in% big) |>
  group_by(scaffold_smiles) |>
  summarise(n = n(), spread = max(pActivity) - min(pActivity),
            weakest = min(pActivity), strongest = max(pActivity),
            mixed_types = any(n_Ki > 0) && any(n_IC50 > 0), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(spread))
cat("scaffold families with >= 5 measured compounds:", nrow(cl),
    "| spanning more than 2 log units:", sum(cl$spread > 2), "\n")
## scaffold families with >= 5 measured compounds: 94 | spanning more than 2 log units: 34
print(as.data.frame(cl |> slice_head(n = 5) |>
  mutate(scaffold_smiles = paste0(str_sub(scaffold_smiles, 1, 32), "\u2026"),
         across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))))
##                     scaffold_smiles   n spread weakest strongest mixed_types
## 1 c1cncc(-c2c[nH]c3nccc(N4CCCCC4)c…  10   4.53    4.30      8.82       FALSE
## 2 O=C(NCc1ccccc1)c1ccc(-c2cn[nH]c2… 207   4.31    5.39      9.70       FALSE
## 3 O=C(NCc1ccccc1)c1ccc(-c2ccncc2)c…  43   4.30    4.80      9.10        TRUE
## 4 c1ncc(-c2c[nH]c3nccc(N4CCCCC4)c2…  24   3.79    4.30      8.09       FALSE
## 5 O=C(NCc1ccccc1)Nc1nc(-c2ccncc2)c…  59   3.76    4.28      8.05       FALSE
cat("\nof the wide families, those mixing Ki and IC50 measurements:",
    sum(cl$mixed_types[cl$spread > 2]), "\n")
## 
## of the wide families, those mixing Ki and IC50 measurements: 6

A fourth observation, offered as a hypothesis rather than a result. Compounds sharing a Bemis–Murcko scaffold are structural relatives, so a family spanning more than two log units contains at least one activity cliff — a small structural change with a large potency consequence.[33][34] Thirty-four of the 94 families with at least five measured compounds qualify, the widest spanning 4.53 log units over only ten compounds. Such compounds are the most informative in a series and the ones that break similarity-based models. They also have a mundane alternative explanation that has to be excluded first: six of these wide families mix Ki and IC50 measurements, and pooling those two quantities is itself a documented source of roughly half a log unit of noise.[30] Telling a real cliff from a measurement artefact needs the structures themselves; the EDA’s job is to find the candidates and label them as candidates.

Bridge

Backwards: Unit 4 (Tidy data in the tidyverse) built the compound table explored here, and Unit 3 downloaded it (Python edition). Forwards: Unit 6 (Data quality, curation and bias) turns the anomalies of Section 11 into quantitative bias diagnostics and a noise floor; Unit 7 attaches uncertainty to the summaries drawn here (Python edition); Unit 20 applies the same EDA discipline to time series, where autocorrelation makes every plot in this unit misleading in a new way (Python edition); and Unit 23 takes these figures to publication quality (Python edition). The R-edition index lists every unit and the Python edition of this unit does the same analysis with matplotlib and seaborn. Sister courses: the chemical meaning of the descriptors plotted here is developed in Unit 5 and the scaffold and chemical-space views in Unit 8 of the cheminformatics course; activity cliffs are the subject of its Unit 11; and the R edition of the AI course covers the modelling that follows, beginning with its R toolkit.

12. Summary

  • EDA is a checklist, not an inspiration: shape and grain, missingness, univariate distributions, pairwise relations, group comparisons, anomalies, write-up. Run it before any model.
  • The grammar of graphics — data, aesthetics, geometry, statistic, scale, facet — turns “which chart?” into a set of explicit choices, and in R ggplot2 is that grammar rather than an analogy to it.
  • Every distribution display has a hidden parameter except the ECDF: bin width for histograms (Scott 0.28, Freedman–Diaconis 0.22 log units here), bandwidth for density estimates, which also leak density past the data’s boundary.
  • Box plots answer one question. Two samples with matched quartiles had entirely different shapes and excess kurtosis −0.01 against −1.22. Draw the points whenever the group is smaller than a few hundred.
  • Overplotting is a measurement problem. At 4,280 points an opaque scatter shows only the silhouette; transparency, 2-D binning (busiest cell: 94 compounds) and subsampling each trade something, and the caption must say which.
  • Correlation matrices show redundancy, not causation. MolWt and HeavyAtoms correlate at 0.979; no descriptor correlates with potency above 0.241.
  • Anscombe’s quartet and the Datasaurus construction are proofs, not anecdotes: three of our generated datasets share five summary statistics to two decimals and look nothing alike.
  • Colour is data encoding. Perceptually uniform maps for quantities, Okabe–Ito for categories, and simulate a colour-vision deficiency before you publish — the ad-hoc palette’s closest pair fell from an RGB distance of 0.23 to 0.08 under deuteranopia, while Okabe–Ito held at 0.20.
  • Three real anomalies in this dataset: value pile-ups at censoring limits and round numbers, including 141 compounds reported at exactly 550 nM by four assays; 470 measurements from 83 assays reported in micromolar, whose median is 2.2 times weaker than the nanomolar-reported ones; and 60 compounds whose replicates disagree by more than a log unit, the worst by 3.3.

13. Self-assessment

  1. What is the one question EDA must answer before any model is fitted?

What is actually in the table — its grain, its gaps, the shape of each variable and the relations between them — so that you know which modelling assumptions are already violated. The secondary purpose is to generate hypotheses; those must then be tested on data not used to find them.

  1. Name the layers of the grammar of graphics and map a 2-D binned density plot onto them.

Data, aesthetic mapping, geometry, statistical transformation, scales, facets, coordinates/theme. The binned plot is: data = the compound table; aesthetics x = MolWt, y = MolLogP, fill = count; geometry = tile; statistic = count of points per rectangular bin; scales = linear axes and a sequential colour map; no facets. In ggplot2 each of those is a separate function call in the same expression.

  1. Why is the ECDF the only distribution display with no tuning parameter, and why is it still not the default?

Because it plots the data themselves: for each observed value, the fraction of observations at or below it. Nothing is binned or smoothed. It is not the default because most readers cannot see a mode in it — the eye reads density far better from a histogram than slope from a cumulative curve.

  1. Your density curve shows mass below the smallest observed value. What happened and what do you do?

The kernel is symmetric and spills past the boundary, assigning density to impossible values. Either state the boundary explicitly and truncate, use a boundary-corrected or reflected kernel, or show an ECDF or histogram instead. Never present the spill as if it were data.

  1. A referee asks you to replace your strip plot of six groups with box plots. When should you refuse?

When the groups are small or unequal, or when any distribution is multimodal or truncated. In Figure 6 family S6 has 16 compounds and S2 is a wall of 23 points against a ceiling at 5.10 — a box plot shows neither. Offer a box overlaid with the points, which satisfies both of you.

  1. Two descriptors correlate at 0.98. What does that mean for an EDA report and for a model?

They carry one piece of information between them. In the report, say so and show one. In a model, the pair makes a linear fit’s coefficients unstable and uninterpretable (collinearity), though it rarely hurts a tree ensemble’s predictions; feature selection or a dimensionality reduction (Unit 13) is the standard response.

  1. What exactly does Anscombe’s quartet prove?

That mean, variance, correlation and the least-squares line are compatible with structurally different data — a linear relation with noise, a parabola, a line plus an outlier, and a vertical stack plus one leverage point. Numerical summaries are necessary and never sufficient; the plot is part of the analysis, not the presentation.

  1. Why is a truncated y axis dishonest on a bar chart but acceptable on a line chart?

Because a bar encodes the value as a length measured from the baseline, so moving the baseline changes the encoded quantity; truncating at 500 made our largest class look 15.2 times the smallest instead of 2.9. A line encodes value as position and the reader reads changes rather than lengths, so a restricted range is a legitimate zoom — provided the axis is labelled.

  1. Why is jet a bad colour map and viridis a good one?

Perceived lightness along jet rises, falls and rises again, so equal data steps are not equal perceptual steps: false boundaries appear at the yellow and cyan bands and real contrast is lost in the green. viridis is constructed to increase monotonically in lightness and to remain distinguishable under the common colour-vision deficiencies, so it also survives greyscale printing.

  1. You find 141 compounds with exactly the same reported potency. What do you do?

Trace them to their source records before anything else — here, one assay reporting a single representative value for 124 compounds of a series. Then record the finding in the data card, treat those compounds as carrying far less information than their count suggests, and make sure the train/test split does not place near-duplicates of the same value on both sides.

  1. Why is “measurements reported in µM are the weak ones” a problem rather than a curiosity?

Because the unit becomes a weak proxy for the experiment type: the micromolar-reported rows are 2.2 times weaker on median than the nanomolar ones. The shift is modest and the distributions overlap, so it is not a label to split on, but it means the reported unit is correlated with the answer — something to record in the data card and to check before treating the pooled set as homogeneous.

  1. How many of the plots in this unit would you put in a paper, and what changes first?

Very few, and that is the point: EDA figures are for you. For publication the changes are a single clear message per figure, axis labels with units, a colour-blind-safe palette, the sample size stated in the panel or caption, and the caption reporting the numbers the reader is meant to take away. Unit 23 does this systematically.

Glossary

Aesthetic mapping
The assignment of data columns to visual channels — position, colour, size, shape, transparency; aes() in ggplot2.
Anti-pattern
A chart convention that reliably misleads: truncated bar axis, dual axis, rainbow colour map, pie with many slices.
Bandwidth
The width of the kernel in a density estimate; the equivalent of bin width, and its hidden parameter (adjust in R’s density()).
Bemis–Murcko scaffold
A molecule reduced to its ring systems and the linkers between them; the standard way of grouping compounds into chemical families.
Clustered heatmap
A heatmap whose rows and columns are reordered by hierarchical clustering so that correlated blocks become contiguous.
Deuteranopia
The commonest colour-vision deficiency, a reduced ability to distinguish red from green; simulated here with the Machado model.
ECDF
Empirical cumulative distribution function: for each value, the fraction of observations at or below it. No tuning parameter.
Exploratory data analysis
Examining data to find structure and generate hypotheses, as distinct from confirmatory analysis, which tests a hypothesis formed beforehand.
Grammar of graphics
The decomposition of a statistical graphic into data, aesthetics, geometry, statistical transformation, scales, facets and coordinates.
Overplotting
So many marks that the ink saturates and density becomes unreadable; treated with transparency, binning or subsampling.
Pile-up
A value shared by far more records than chance allows, usually a reporting convention rather than a measurement.
Small multiples
One small plot repeated across the levels of a variable with shared axes, so the panels are directly comparable; facet_wrap().
